newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eurostar rail firms mull Eurotunnel claims.
newsitem.headline: Eurostar rail firms mull Eurotunnel claims.

text.p: Distressed Channel Tunnel operator Eurotunnel SA/Plc on Monday faced potential claims from companies running the Eurostar high-speed train after a fire last week shut down passenger services.

Britain's Eurostar UK, France's SNCF and Belgium's SNCB railway companies are losing revenues every day the tunnel is closed to passengers and the latter two told Reuters they are considering compensation claims. The British firm said it has a compensation agreement with Eurotunnel, but denied a London newspaper report the claim could be 10 million stg.
Eurotunnel officials were not available for comment.
"The fire couldn't come at a worse time," said analyst Scott Bugie at debt rating agency Standard & Poor's in Paris.
The fire, which started on board a truck on a freight service late on Monday night last week, threatens to take Eurotunnel out of service for the busy Christmas period.
It comes at a time when lead banks in its 225-strong bank syndicate are trying to muster 100 percent support for a complex restructuring of its 70 billion francs junior bank debt.

The company's revenue forecasts for next year will likely be upset as insurance claims and counterclaims are filed for operating losses, infrastructure damage and managers consider potential equipment redesign.
Meanwhile, shareholders are being asked to approve the refinancing, which threatens to dilute their holdings massively in a debt-for-equity swap with the banks.
The expected claims from the Eurostar operators can only mean more demands on management time.

"The SNCF is suffering a commercial prejudice as it is unable to operate the Eurostar," an SNCF spokesman said. "Naturally it expects to be compensated and is currently studying the possibilities open to it."
The SNCF spokesman could not estimate the losses or the size of any claim against Eurotunnel other than say the amounts ran into "several million francs per day."
Some 19,000 Eurostar tickets were being sold daily since the beginning of November, he added.
Eurotunnel is insured for operating losses and infrastructure damage with French insurer UAP.
French newspaper Le Monde reported the insurance does not cover the minimum usage fee that Eurotunnel receives from the railway companies for booking half the Tunnel capacity.
The UAP spokesman said it was too early to put any figures to any Eurotunnel claim as the company and UAP are still in the process of evaluating the damage from last week's fire.
"The process will take several days or weeks," he said.
In London, Eurostar UK said it has a compensation agreement that allows it to claim if it is unable to use the Tunnel.
"We have a contractual agreement with Eurotunnel which provides for the partial or complete unavailability of the tunnel," a company spokesman said.
He denied a report in the London Evening Standard newspaper the claim might be for 10 million stg.

Eurostar had been running up to 24 return services from London to Paris and Brussels a day. Before the fire, demand was running at 6.4 million passengers a year, up from around 3.9 million a year ago. But senior executives said earlier this month they needed over 10 million passengers a year to put Eurostar into profit.

Eurostar UK is owned by the London and Continental Railways (L&CR) consortium, which includes bus transport firm National Express, British entrepreneur Richard Branson's Virgin Group, investment bank SBC Warburg, U.S. project management specialist Bechtel and civil engineering consultants Ove Arup and Halcrow.
In Brussels, Belgian National Railways said it was considering suing Eurotunnel for damages.
"We are investigating what is possible, together with our partners and individually," NMBS director Leo Pardon told Belgian VTM television."
-- Pierre Tran, Paris newsroom +33 1 4221 5452
